source.name: Python for Everybody by Charles Severance

course.title: Programming Foundations with Python
course.description: Learn to program in Python by writing real code in your browser: values and variables, functions, loops, lists, and strings — every concept practiced against automated tests that run instantly, with no setup. Structure informed by the open course Python for Everybody by Charles Severance (CC BY-NC-SA 3.0).

questions.prompt: Which function shows a value on the screen in Python?
questions.explanation: print() writes its arguments to standard output — the main way to display results in Python.

questions.prompt: What does the expression 3 + 4 * 2 evaluate to in Python?
questions.explanation: Multiplication binds tighter than addition, so 4*2 = 8 is computed first, then 3 + 8 = 11.

questions.prompt: What type does the expression 10 / 3 produce in Python 3?
questions.explanation: In Python 3 the / operator always produces a float; use // for integer (floor) division.

questions.prompt: How do you define a function in Python?
questions.explanation: The def keyword introduces a function, followed by its name, parameters, and a colon.

questions.prompt: The list [10, 20, 30] has its value 20 at which index?
questions.explanation: Lists are zero-indexed: index 0 is 10, index 1 is 20, index 2 is 30.

questions.prompt: What makes a block of code 'inside' a function or loop in Python?
questions.explanation: Python uses indentation (whitespace), not braces, to define which lines belong to a block.

lessons.title: Values, variables, and expressions
lessons.grammar_note: Python is indentation-sensitive: the lines that belong to a function or loop are the ones indented beneath it. Be consistent — four spaces per level is the convention.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Read and predict the result of simple Python expressions, and store results in variables. Warm-up: what do you think "5" + "1" produces in Python?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: A program manipulates values. The types you meet first are integers (42), floats (3.14), strings of text ("hello"), and booleans (True, False — capitalized in Python). An expression is any fragment that produces a value: 3 + 4 produces 7. A variable gives a value a name with =, so x = 10 binds the name x to 10. Operators combine values: + adds numbers but joins (concatenates) strings, so "5" + "1" is "51", not 6. Unlike some languages, Python will not let you add a string and a number directly — "5" + 1 raises a TypeError.

sections.heading: Worked examples
sections.text: price = 20; with_tax = price * 1.1 leaves with_tax as 22.0 (a float). The remainder operator % gives what is left after division: 10 % 3 is 1. Integer division // discards the fraction: 10 // 3 is 3. Booleans come from comparisons: 5 > 3 is True, 5 == 5 is True, 5 == "5" is False because an int and a str are never equal. Strings concatenate to build messages: name = "Sam"; greeting = "Hi, " + name gives "Hi, Sam".

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: writing true/false in lowercase — Python spells them True and False. Mistake: expecting / to give a whole number; in Python 3 use // for that. Exit: (a) What does "3" + "4" produce? (b) What does 7 // 2 produce? Answers: the string "34"; 3.

body.prompt: Write a function square(n) that returns n multiplied by itself.
body.instructions: In Python, def introduces a function and return hands a value back. Mind the indentation — the body is indented under the def line. Click Run & check; the lesson unlocks when all tests pass. (The first run downloads the Python runtime once.)

lessons.title: Functions, arguments, and return
lessons.grammar_note: A Python function with no return statement returns None. Returning a value and printing a value are different — return hands data back to the caller; print only displays it.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Define functions that take arguments and return results, and explain the difference between returning and printing. Warm-up: if a function has no return statement, what value does calling it produce?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: A function is a reusable piece of a program with a name, parameters, and an indented body. def add(a, b): return a + b defines add; add(2, 3) calls it and produces 5. Parameters (a, b) are local names for the values passed in. The moment a return runs, the function stops and its value becomes the result of the call. A function that never returns gives back None. print() is different: it displays a value but does not hand it back, so total = print(5) leaves total as None.

sections.heading: Worked examples
sections.text: def greet(name): return "Hello, " + name + "!" — greet("Ada") produces "Hello, Ada!". Functions can make decisions: def sign(n): if n > 0: return "positive"; if n < 0: return "negative"; return "zero". Because return stops the function, sign(5) returns "positive" and never checks the other branches. Functions can call other functions: def fourth_power(n): return square(square(n)) reuses square from the previous lesson.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: Decide what each returns. 1) def f(x): return x + 1  ->  f(9). 2) def g(): pass  ->  g(). 3) def h(a, b): return a > b  ->  h(3, 5). 4) def k(n): if n % 2 == 0: return "even"; return "odd"  ->  k(7). Answers: 1) 10. 2) None. 3) False. 4) "odd".

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: forgetting return, so the function computes a value and then discards it (returns None). Mistake: confusing print with return — print shows a value but does not give it back to be used. Exit: (a) What does add(4, 4) return for def add(a, b): return a + b? (b) What does a function with no return give back? Answers: 8; None.

body.prompt: Write sum_to(n) that returns 1 + 2 + 3 + ... + n. If n is 0 or less, return 0.
body.instructions: Keep a running total in a variable and add each number to it. Hint: range(1, n + 1) counts from 1 up to n. Watch your indentation.
body.starter:
def sum_to(n):
    total = 0
    # loop from 1 to n and add each to total
    return total

lessons.title: Lists and iteration
lessons.grammar_note: List indexes start at 0, so the last index of a list of length n is n - 1. Reading past the end raises an IndexError rather than returning a quiet value.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Store lists of values, read and change elements by index, and walk through a list with a loop. Warm-up: for the list [7, 8, 9], what is the index of 9?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: A list is an ordered collection written in square brackets: xs = [7, 8, 9]. Each element has an index starting at 0, so xs[0] is 7 and xs[2] is 9. The number of elements is len(xs). You can loop directly over the values with for x in xs, or over positions with for i in range(len(xs)). Lists have useful methods: xs.append(10) adds to the end, and the in operator asks whether a value is present: 8 in xs is True.

sections.heading: Worked examples
sections.text: Summing a list: def total(xs): s = 0; for x in xs: s += x; return s  ->  total([1, 2, 3]) is 6. Finding the largest: def biggest(xs): m = xs[0]; for x in xs: if x > m: m = x; return m  ->  biggest([3, 9, 4]) is 9. Building a new list: def doubled(xs): out = []; for x in xs: out.append(x * 2); return out  ->  doubled([1, 2, 3]) is [2, 4, 6]. Reading xs[len(xs)] raises IndexError because the last valid index is len(xs) - 1.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: Given xs = [4, 8, 15, 16]: 1) What is len(xs)? 2) What is xs[0] + xs[3]? 3) What is the last valid index? 4) After xs.append(23), what is len(xs)? 5) Is 15 in xs? Answers: 1) 4. 2) 20. 3) 3. 4) 5. 5) True.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: looping with range(len(xs) + 1), which runs one step too far and raises IndexError. Mistake: assuming the last index equals len; it is len - 1. Exit: (a) What is the first index of any non-empty list? (b) How do you get the number of elements? Answers: 0; len(xs).

body.prompt: Write evens_only(xs) that returns a NEW list containing only the even numbers from xs, in their original order. Do not change the input list.
body.instructions: Build up a new list with append. Keep a number only if it is even (x % 2 == 0). Leave the input list untouched.
body.starter:
def evens_only(xs):
    out = []
    # add each even number of xs to out
    return out

questions.prompt: What does the expression 10 % 3 evaluate to?
questions.explanation: % is the remainder operator: 10 divided by 3 leaves 1.
len is 3, so the last index is 3 - 1 = 2, holding 7.

questions.prompt: What does range(1, 4) produce values for?
questions.explanation: range(a, b) counts from a up to but NOT including b, so range(1, 4) yields 1, 2, 3.

questions.prompt: What does this function return: def f(n): \n if n > 0: return "+" \n return "-"  called as f(0)?
questions.explanation: 0 is not greater than 0, so the first return is skipped and the function returns "-".

questions.prompt: Which builds a new list without changing the original?
options: Appending to a fresh out list
questions.explanation: Creating a separate out list and appending to it leaves the input untouched.
Strings have a length too: "code" has 4 characters.

body.instructions: Lowercase the string first with s.lower(), then check each character. Hint: ch in "aeiou" tells you whether ch is a vowel. You can loop over a string with for ch in s.
body.starter:
def count_vowels(s):

body.prompt: Write fizzbuzz(n): return 'Fizz' if n is divisible by 3, 'Buzz' if divisible by 5, 'FizzBuzz' if divisible by both, otherwise the number as a string (use str(n)).
body.instructions: This classic exercise ties together conditionals, the remainder operator, and returning strings. Check the both-divisible case first — order matters.
